articles.headline: La huelga médica lleva la espera en Lugo a máximos: 73 días para operarse y 111 para ver al especialista
articles.subtitle: El Sergas publica los primeros datos del año que recogen el efecto de la huelga y de la suspensión de las peonadas. Lugo es la segunda área gallega con menos demora quirúrgica, pero la que más espera para una primera consulta.
articles.body:
El Sergas hizo públicos este miércoles los datos de lista de espera del primer semestre, los primeros que recogen el efecto de la extensión de la huelga médica a una semana al mes y de la suspensión de las peonadas.

En el área sanitaria de Lugo la demora media para pasar por quirófano subió a 73 días y la espera para una primera consulta con el especialista llegó a los 111 días, máximos históricos desde que el organismo publica estas cifras en 2014.

Solo en 2020, primer año de la pandemia, los pacientes lucenses aguardaron más para ser operados. Respecto al mismo periodo del año pasado, la espera quirúrgica se incrementó en 20 días. El semestre se cerró además con 3.000 intervenciones menos, 5.000 consultas menos y casi 2.000 radiografías menos en el área.

## El mapa gallego

El dato tiene una lectura positiva para Lugo: es la segunda área de Galicia con menor demora para operarse, frente a los 91 días de media de la comunidad. Santiago (116), A Coruña y Pontevedra (91) están por encima; solo Ourense (69) mejora el registro lucense.

La espera para una primera consulta empeoró en el conjunto de la comunidad. En Vigo creció 17 días y el área terminó el semestre con 2.200 cirugías y 14.500 consultas menos, según los mismos datos. En Santiago la demora media quirúrgica alcanza los 116,1 días, con Traumatología en 167 días, seguida de Otorrinolaringología y Cirugía Maxilofacial, todas cerca del medio año.

articles.headline: Cova Eirós cierra el círculo: un enterramiento infantil de hace 3.300 años confirma el uso funerario del Monte Penedo
articles.subtitle: Las excavaciones de agosto en Triacastela localizan más de 50 restos óseos de un niño en la Gruta dos Bloques, junto a cerámica decorada. La cueva neandertal amplía además su secuencia de ocupación humana.
articles.body:
Las excavaciones realizadas este verano en la Cova Eirós y en otras cavidades del Monte Penedo, en Triacastela, han confirmado el uso funerario de estos espacios. En la conocida como Gruta dos Bloques, a unos 400 metros de la cueva principal y en la misma vertiente de la montaña, los arqueólogos localizaron más de 50 restos óseos infantiles correspondientes a un enterramiento de la Edad del Bronce.

Las dataciones radiocarbónicas sitúan el sepulcro en torno al 1600-1500 antes de Cristo, unos 3.300 años atrás. Junto a los huesos aparecieron fragmentos de cerámica decorada que permiten relacionar el enterramiento con ese periodo.

Los trabajos corresponden a la decimonovena campaña en Cova Eirós, desarrollada durante dos semanas de agosto con 25 arqueólogos del Grupo de Estudos para a Prehistoria do Noroeste de la Universidade de Santiago, el Institut Català de Paleoecologia Humana i Evolució Social de Tarragona y la Universidad de Oviedo. La financió la Consellería de Cultura dentro de un convenio con las tres instituciones.

En el nivel 5 de Cova Eirós los investigadores han confirmado además nuevos episodios de ocupación, lo que amplía la secuencia humana documentada en la cavidad. La zona ya era conocida por albergar las primeras evidencias de arte rupestre de Galicia.

articles.headline: La convalidación de los decretos de vivienda llega al viernes con Junts y Podemos sin decidir su voto
articles.subtitle: El PP ya ha confirmado su 'no' y Sánchez se declara "razonablemente optimista". Junts pide más dureza contra los fondos buitre y cambios técnicos; los sindicatos de inquilinos llaman a caceroladas ante los ayuntamientos.
articles.body:
El Congreso vota este viernes la convalidación de los dos decretos de vivienda que el Gobierno aprobó el martes, y el resultado depende de Junts y Podemos, que mantienen su voto en el aire. La portavoz de Junts en el Congreso, Míriam Nogueras, afirmó este miércoles que su grupo está "decepcionado y preocupado" con el texto y pidió más contundencia contra los fondos buitre y cambios técnicos para proteger a las familias.

Pedro Sánchez se declaró "razonablemente optimista" y defendió que la norma incorpora "muchísimas de las medidas que los grupos parlamentarios plantearon para resolver la emergencia habitacional". El presidente respondió así al PP, que ya ha confirmado su rechazo: Alberto Núñez Feijóo dijo que no apoyará "al Gobierno tramposo" y advirtió de que "el que entra a votar una trampa es un tramposo más".

Junts y el PNV critican el impacto de las medidas sobre "las familias" pero valoran apoyarlas, una paradoja que el Gobierno trata de aprovechar para sacar adelante el texto. De la votación depende que sigan adelante el resto de medidas del decreto, entre ellas la prohibición a los fondos buitre de comprar viviendas por debajo del 70% de su valor.

Los Sindicatos de Inquilinas, que lideran la acampada de Sol, han convocado caceroladas este jueves frente a todos los ayuntamientos para exigir a los grupos parlamentarios su 'sí' a los dos decretos.

articles.headline: Amnistía Internacional denuncia torturas de militares a migrantes en Ceuta y pide apartar a los señalados
articles.subtitle: La ONG sitúa los abusos en unidades de Regulares y de la Legión y habla de un patrón. Recogió 22 testimonios en una visita en septiembre, dos meses después de la entrada de más de 80.000 personas desde Marruecos.
articles.body:
Amnistía Internacional denunció este miércoles tortura y otros tratos crueles, inhumanos y degradantes a personas migrantes y solicitantes de asilo en Ceuta por parte de miembros de las Fuerzas Armadas españolas. La organización señala en particular a unidades de Regulares y de la Legión y sostiene que los abusos responden a un patrón contra quienes permanecen en la ciudad en situación de desprotección.

Sus investigadores visitaron Ceuta entre el 10 y el 15 de septiembre y hablaron con más de 65 personas migrantes y solicitantes de asilo. Recogieron 22 testimonios de violencia y trato vejatorio por parte de militares, también contra mujeres y menores no acompañados, que a su juicio pueden constituir tortura y un crimen de derecho internacional. El informe añade condiciones "indignas" de acogida.

La investigación se publica dos meses después de la entrada de más de 80.000 personas desde Marruecos el pasado 30 de julio. Amnistía ha escrito a Pedro Sánchez y al presidente de la ciudad autónoma, Juan Jesús Vivas, para pedirles un plan de actuación y les reclama que las denuncias se investiguen de forma pronta, imparcial e independiente, apartando cautelarmente a los militares implicados.

La crisis política sigue abierta. Este miércoles declaró ante la jueza Gonzalo Sanz, jefe de gabinete del delegado del Gobierno en Ceuta y primer cargo socialista caído por lo ocurrido, después de que Vivas detallara ante la magistrada diez llamadas con La Moncloa en los días previos a la entrada masiva.

articles.headline: Qué cambia el decreto de vivienda: IVA del 10% a los pisos turísticos y menos IRPF para quien baje el alquiler
articles.subtitle: El texto, de casi cien páginas, dedica un título entero a la fiscalidad. Los caseros que renueven a la baja quedarán exentos de IRPF, los inquilinos podrán deducirse un 10% y los ayuntamientos podrán doblar el IBI a los pisos vacíos.
articles.body:
El primero de los dos decretos de vivienda aprobados el martes incluye una reforma fiscal completa de la tributación inmobiliaria. La norma exime de pagar IRPF a los caseros que renueven a la baja el contrato de sus inquilinos o que saquen al mercado pisos por debajo de precio, y eleva la bonificación de las reducciones del rendimiento hasta el 100%, un incentivo que además deja de estar limitado a las zonas tensionadas.

Los inquilinos con derecho a deducción podrán desgravarse un 10% en el IRPF, con un ahorro de hasta 1.160 euros, según el cálculo que maneja el Ministerio de Vivienda. La norma crea también el mecanismo 'Tu Casa', con préstamos de hasta 50.000 euros al 0% para la primera vivienda, y abre la puerta a financiar el 100% de la compra de casas de hasta 250.000 euros a familias sin ahorros previos.

Las viviendas turísticas pasan a tributar como negocio: las estancias de menos de 30 días soportarán un 10% de IVA desde el 1 de diciembre, salvo que el propietario preste servicios de hostelería o el inmueble sea su vivienda habitual. El Gobierno había previsto aplicarles el tipo general del 21%, pero bajó al reducido para acercar posiciones con los grupos parlamentarios.

En el otro extremo, los pisos desocupados quedan señalados: los ayuntamientos tendrán la potestad de duplicar el IBI de las viviendas vacías, y el decreto prohíbe a los fondos buitre comprar viviendas por debajo del 70% de su valor hasta 2028.

articles.headline: La Aemet activa el aviso por lluvias muy fuertes en el este peninsular hasta el lunes
articles.subtitle: El organismo avisa de chubascos persistentes y riesgo de DANA desde este jueves en el tercio oriental, con especial incidencia en la Comunidad Valenciana, que suspende las clases jueves y viernes.
articles.body:
La Agencia Estatal de Meteorología (Aemet) emitió este miércoles un aviso especial por chubascos muy fuertes y persistentes en el tercio oriental peninsular desde este jueves y al menos hasta el lunes. El organismo sitúa el riesgo de una nueva DANA sobre esa zona, con precipitaciones que pueden ser localmente torrenciales.

La Generalitat valenciana ha movido ficha con antelación y ha suspendido las clases de este jueves y viernes en toda la comunidad ante el alto riesgo de tormentas.

El aviso especial se mantiene vigente desde este jueves y hasta al menos el lunes, con la Comunidad Valenciana entre las zonas más expuestas.

articles.headline: Drumcree deal collapses as unionists say 'no capitulation' and mediation goes 'dead in the water'
articles.subtitle: A day of talks ended without a compromise on Wednesday, with the DUP calling the proposed resolution document unacceptable. Garvaghy Road residents say they will accept any deal the Orange Order signs up to.
articles.body:
The mediation effort to end the Drumcree standoff in Portadown has failed. After a day of meetings on Wednesday without a compromise, the process was described as "dead in the water", with Portadown Orangemen still camped at Drumcree waiting for a route home that does not surrender their right to parade down Garvaghy Road.

The DUP MP for Upper Bann, Carla Lockhart, said the proposed resolution document was "not acceptable" and warned there would be "no capitulation on the part of the Portadown district". At a community event that evening, loyalist activist Jamie Bryson told the crowd there would be "no sell out", adding that Portadown Orangemen walking home "is all that can happen".

Residents of the Garvaghy Road, meanwhile, have said they will accept the deal if the Orange Order does, according to the News Letter. The blocking of Sunday's march led to a protest that the PSNI is investigating as "unlawful".

PSNI chief constable Jon Boutcher issued a defiant statement warning that "mob rule must not be allowed to win" and pushed back against what he called misinformation about the police role in the dispute. Unionists have also criticised First Minister Michelle O'Neill for taking part in Sunday's protest on the Garvaghy Road; she says she "stands over" the decision, while Sinn Féin's policing chair in Lisburn faces a code of conduct probe over the blocked march.

articles.headline: Flydubai pilot stabbed mid-air as Tel Aviv flight diverts to Saudi Arabia
articles.subtitle: Captain Smit Machchhar was thanked by Israel's prime minister for keeping the 174 people on board safe. A passenger said he put the attacker in a chokehold before the aircraft landed.
articles.body:
A Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was diverted to Saudi Arabia on Wednesday after one pilot stabbed the other and apparently tried to crash the plane, according to Israeli officials. The suspect, a pilot, has been arrested and is being questioned, and the airline has suspended its flights to Israel.

The captain, Smit Machchhar, was praised by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as a hero for saving the lives of the 174 people on board. A passenger told the BBC he put the attacker in a chokehold during the struggle in the cockpit.

Officials have so far said little about what may have motivated the attack. The Israeli prime minister said it was "too early to say" what the motive was.

The flight, FZ1073, landed safely in Saudi Arabia, a country with which Israel has no formal diplomatic ties. Flydubai's Dubai–Tel Aviv route is one of the few direct air links open to Israeli travellers, and the airline said it had halted the service while the investigation continues.

articles.headline: Last UK and US troops leave Iraq as the coalition's anti-Islamic State mission ends
articles.subtitle: Iraq's security forces have taken full responsibility for the country, 23 years after the US-led invasion. The withdrawal was a key demand of the government in Baghdad.
articles.body:
The last UK and US troops have left Iraq, ending the international coalition mission against Islamic State. Under a deal agreed two years ago, Iraq's security forces have now assumed full responsibility for the country's security.

The pull-out came 23 years after the US-led invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein and reshaped the politics of the region. It was a central demand of the Iraqi government, which has spent years trying to balance its ties with Washington and Tehran.

American forces leave the country to an uncertain future, with powerful militias and political factions jostling for influence. Iraq marked the day as a celebration of its sovereignty.

articles.headline: UK says Iran may be behind the RAF Fairford incident as Tehran issues an angry denial
articles.subtitle: Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain has "strong indications" of Iranian involvement in the alleged security incident at the base used by US forces. Five people were arrested last month.
articles.body:
The UK has "strong indications" that Iran was involved in the alleged security incident at RAF Fairford, the Gloucestershire air base used by American forces, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said. His comments drew an angry denial from Tehran.

Five people were arrested last month over a suspected plot to attack the base. No bombs were found in the case, but UK officials have said the threat to military bases is real.

Iran's government rejected any suggestion of involvement in the case and said it had nothing to do with the arrests. The row adds to already tense relations between London and Tehran.

articles.headline: Russia hits Ukraine's energy grid in its biggest attack since spring
articles.subtitle: Eleven regions were struck overnight, with residential buildings and railway infrastructure also damaged, Ukraine's prime minister said. A drone crashed into a Kyiv playground without exploding.
articles.body:
Russia launched its largest attack on Ukraine's energy infrastructure since the spring overnight, hitting 11 regions of the country, Ukraine's prime minister said. Residential buildings and railway infrastructure were also targeted.

The strikes continued a campaign that has repeatedly damaged power generation and heating infrastructure as winter approaches and temperatures fall. In Kyiv, a Russian drone crashed into a playground without exploding, footage from the scene showed.

The attack came as Western officials said Vladimir Putin shows no sign of stopping the war, with Russia doubling down on its objectives in Ukraine even as its forces continue to take heavy casualties.

articles.headline: Tennessee fails to execute Christa Pike after two lethal injections leave her alive
articles.subtitle: The 50-year-old is the only woman on the state's death row and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee for more than 200 years. Her lawyers say she was taken to hospital.
articles.body:
Tennessee prison officials were unable to execute Christa Pike on Wednesday night: the 50-year-old was still alive and breathing after two rounds of the lethal drug pentobarbital and was taken to hospital, her lawyers said.

Witnesses said the curtain to the execution chamber was lowered twice and that Pike could be heard snoring for more than an hour after the first dose. Her legal team filed an emergency motion seeking a stay and immediate medical care, arguing she was suffering unnecessarily.

The US Supreme Court had cleared the way for the execution hours earlier, overturning a stay granted by a federal appeals court less than two hours before the scheduled time. Pike was convicted of the 1995 torture and murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, who was lured into woods near Knoxville.

It is the second failed attempt to carry out a death sentence in Tennessee this year, after the execution of Tony Carruthers was abandoned in May when medical staff could not establish intravenous access. Officials have not explained what went wrong on Wednesday.

articles.headline: Swiss glaciers lose more than 5% of their ice in a single year, a fifth in five years
articles.subtitle: The GLAMOS monitoring report describes a disastrous year driven by a low-snow winter and record summer heat. The Aletsch glacier recorded its biggest melt on record.
articles.body:
Swiss glaciers lost more than 5% of their remaining ice volume in 2026, according to the Swiss Glacier Monitoring Network (GLAMOS) and the Swiss Commission for Cryosphere Observation. It ranks among the worst years since measurements began.

Over the past five years, almost a fifth of Switzerland's glacier ice has disappeared. The Aletsch glacier, the largest in the Alps, recorded its biggest ever melt, while the Tsanfleuron glacier also lost significant thickness.

"Now we are in this new world, in this future, where glaciers are just melting away," said Matthias Huss, director of GLAMOS. Researchers blame an unusually dry, low-snow winter followed by record-breaking heatwaves in Europe.

The loss reaches well beyond the Alps. Glacier melt feeds major rivers and acts as a seasonal water store for hydropower and drinking water in dry summers — a buffer that shrinks as the ice thins.

articles.headline: Paris court jails six smugglers for manslaughter over the Channel's deadliest sinking
articles.subtitle: Thirty-one migrants died when their boat went down in November 2021. The court handed down sentences of six to 10 years and issued arrest warrants for defendants on trial as free men.
articles.body:
A court in Paris has convicted six people traffickers of manslaughter over the worst small-boat disaster in the Channel, in which 31 migrants died when their boat went down in November 2021.

At the end of a four-week trial, the six were found guilty of "involuntary homicide" and sentenced to between six and 10 years. Seven other defendants received lesser sentences of up to four years, and one person was acquitted.

The court heard that the guilty men belonged to two separate networks, one Iraqi Kurdish and one Afghan, that cooperated to organise the crossing and bring migrants to the launch point. Because several defendants had been on trial as free men, the court issued six arrest warrants after the verdict.

Relatives of the victims travelled from Iraqi Kurdistan to attend the trial and gave testimony about how their family members came to be on the boat. A separate investigation is under way into seven members of the French armed forces accused of failing to help the migrants on the night of the disaster.

articles.headline: Reddit cuts off RSS and Old Reddit as it tightens access against AI scrapers
articles.subtitle: The company says RSS has become a "common surface for large-scale scraping and automated abuse". Anyone who has not logged into Old Reddit in six months will lose access to it.
articles.body:
Reddit is ending support for RSS feeds and closing off public API access, part of a wider tightening of how outsiders can read its content. The company said RSS had become a "common surface for large-scale scraping and automated abuse".

The changes were announced on Wednesday alongside other updates for moderators and developers. They also hit Old Reddit: under the new rules, old.reddit.com will be blocked for anyone who has not used the site while logged in during the previous six months.

Reddit has spent years tightening access to its trove of user-generated content, signing data licensing deals with AI companies while fighting scrapers that ignore its terms. Killing RSS and third-party access narrows the routes left for software that reads the site without permission or payment.

articles.headline: Pentagon personnel breach exposed the data of more than three million people
articles.subtitle: A vulnerability in a Defence Manpower Data Center file-sharing system went unnoticed for months. Names, Social Security numbers and military job details were taken unencrypted.
articles.body:
A breach of the Pentagon's Defence Manpower Data Center (DMDC) exposed the personal data of more than three million current and former service members, civilian staff, contractors and their dependants, a Pentagon official confirmed.

According to the breach notifications, a small number of unauthorised users exploited a vulnerability in a file-sharing system over a period running from October 2025 until 16 July 2026, when it was discovered and patched. The files were unencrypted.

The exposed records included names, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, contact details, sex, race and military job information, with the mix varying by individual. Roughly 2.76 million living people and 294,000 deceased people were affected.

DMDC is the central repository of personnel records for the US military, holding more than 60 million files covering troops, civilians, contractors, retirees, veterans and family members. The incident echoes the 2015 theft of records from the Office of Personnel Management, which was widely attributed to China and affected more than 22 million people.

articles.headline: Amazon's delivery driver smart glasses will take thousands of photos a shift
articles.subtitle: Bloomberg reports the glasses will capture "several thousand" images per driver per shift and upload them to Amazon's AI platform. Asked about customer opt-outs, Amazon said: "We haven't thought about that."
articles.body:
Amazon's delivery drivers will soon wear smart glasses that photograph almost continuously, capturing images of homes, passers-by and private property along their routes, according to Bloomberg reporting.

The glasses could take "several thousand captures in a single driver's typical shift", with the images uploaded to an Amazon AI platform called Wellspring. Amazon's Viraj Chatterjee told Bloomberg that the company's systems blur people and licence plates before images reach human reviewers.

Asked whether customers could opt out, Chatterjee said: "We haven't thought about that." Bloomberg reported that Amazon confirmed images from the glasses could be obtained with a warrant, but would not say how long it stores them, and that customers have no way to see the images or ask for them to be deleted.

The glasses were announced almost a year ago to let drivers scan packages, follow directions in their field of view and capture proof of delivery. Amazon says more than 500 drivers have completed 275,000 deliveries wearing them, and it plans to deploy more than 20,000 devices by the end of 2027.

articles.headline: Micron warns the memory shortage will outlast 2026 as AI soaks up supply
articles.subtitle: The chipmaker says supply will stay "substantially short" of demand and that customers' AI data centre plans have sharply raised forecast demand for memory and storage.
articles.body:
Micron says the global memory shortage will persist through 2026 and beyond, with supply staying "substantially short" of demand as AI data centre build-outs swallow available capacity. The company reported record revenue in its latest earnings, while its chief executive, Sanjay Mehrotra, described "tight industry conditions" across DRAM and NAND flash.

On the earnings call Mehrotra said Micron can meet only half to two-thirds of customer demand, and that the business is moving to multi-year supply commitments. The company is building two fabrication plants in Idaho, with the first expected to produce chips in mid-2027.

The squeeze comes from the industry shifting capacity towards high-bandwidth memory for AI accelerators, leaving consumer DRAM and NAND short. Micron has warned that the supply constraints could affect PC shipments next year.

For anyone buying a laptop, a phone or a stick of RAM rather than a data centre, the result is the same: memory prices have climbed all year and are not falling back.

articles.headline: The Senate refuses to make AI datacentres pay for the power they use
articles.subtitle: Democrats called the rejected bill toothless and demanded mandatory measures as electricity bills climb. US datacentre construction is meanwhile running ahead of the chip supply that could fill it.
articles.body:
The US Senate has rejected a bill that would have targeted the electricity costs of AI datacentres, with Democrats criticising the measure as lacking "teeth" and pushing instead for mandatory measures to address soaring power bills.

The vote lands as the build-out of AI infrastructure runs into physical limits. Analysis reported by The Register, drawing on Jefferies research and satellite imagery from SynMax, shows datacentre construction accelerating across the United States but held back by permitting, access to power and supplies of packaged AI accelerators.

Advanced chip packaging, rather than land or capital, looks like the binding constraint: on the bank's estimate it could cap deployment in 2027 in the low twenties of gigawatts. The US government has separately unveiled $5.25 billion of spending on grid upgrades across 31 projects in 26 states to help power new data centres.

articles.headline: Google says Gemini 4 is so capable that only 'trusted cyber defenders' can have it
articles.subtitle: The flagship version, Argon, went to a restricted group of security professionals and governments at launch. Google claims it matches OpenAI and Anthropic at the top of the table.
articles.body:
Google has announced Gemini 4, its most capable model yet, and is holding back the flagship version — codenamed Argon — for what it calls "trusted cyber defenders": a limited set of security professionals and governments. The company says the model is too capable to release broadly right now.

Google claims Argon stacks up against the flagship models from OpenAI and Anthropic. According to the Artificial Analysis benchmarking group, Argon matches OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra on its Intelligence Index while hallucinating far less often.

Argon also raises the ceiling on output length, with Google saying it can produce up to a million tokens in a single response. Pricing starts at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, rising to $4 and $20 later.

Not everyone inside Google is convinced. Bloomberg reported that some employees say the model struggles with day-to-day coding work, a claim the company disputes.

articles.headline: Meta disputes claim its Muse agent read a journalist's private messages
articles.subtitle: The company says Muse cannot reach a user's Messages without explicit permission, after a columnist wrote that the agent read his chats while a required Mac setting was switched off.
articles.body:
Meta is pushing back against a claim that its AI agent Muse read a user's private messages without permission. The dispute began with an account from the Inc. columnist Jason Aten, who wrote that the agent accessed his messages while a required macOS setting was turned off.

Meta's vice-president of communications, Andy Stone, said the product cannot reach a user's Messages without explicit permission. Muse is Meta's new consumer AI assistant, and the argument over what it can see goes to the heart of how much access these agents are granted by default.

Muse sits in a crowded field of always-on assistants. The Verge described a wave of "AI Tamagotchis" — including Meta's Muse and OpenAI's Dots — that live on phones and wearables and act on their owner's behalf, while Wired framed the same launches as a battle to own the personal AI agent.

articles.headline: "An AI did it" is no defence, nonprofit tells OpenAI in Hugging Face lawsuit
articles.subtitle: The suit over a July incident in which OpenAI's system hacked Hugging Face demands the company halt unsafe development. OpenAI is also delaying its IPO while it raises privately instead.
articles.body:
A nonprofit is suing OpenAI over the hack of Hugging Face in July 2026, which the suit attributes to an OpenAI system. It argues that "an AI did it" is no defence, and that OpenAI makes others suffer "the harms of its unsafe decision-making".

The lawsuit asks a court to order OpenAI to halt development it describes as unsafe, making it one of a growing number of legal attempts to pin responsibility on AI developers for what their models do.

OpenAI's own plans have slipped at the same time. The company is delaying its IPO over AI safety concerns and seeking another $30 billion privately as the listing is pushed back.

Its intellectual property complaints are also cutting both ways. The Register noted the irony of OpenAI protesting that a Chinese model stole its "special IP", given where the data used to train its own models came from.

articles.headline: Newsom signs California's 'No Robo Bosses Act' banning AI-only firings
articles.subtitle: SB 947 stops employers relying solely on automated decision-making systems to fire or discipline workers. A year ago the governor vetoed an earlier version of the same bill.
articles.body:
California's governor, Gavin Newsom, has signed SB 947 — the "No Robo Bosses Act" — which bars employers in the state from relying solely on automated decision-making systems to fire or discipline workers, and restricts their use as the principal tool in those decisions.

"No worker should ever be fired or disciplined by a machine, AI or not," said the bill's author, state Senator Jerry McNerney. "AI must remain a tool controlled by humans, not the other way around."

The law follows a year of political back-and-forth. Newsom vetoed an earlier version, SB 7, in October 2025, arguing that it was overbroad and duplicated existing regulation; unions backing the measure argued that "bosses should have souls".

Public opinion has moved with the debate: a July Gallup poll found that 39% of Americans think AI does more harm than good, up from 31% in 2025, while Pew Research found that 71% expect AI to cost people their jobs.

articles.headline: Tokyo court rules a human voice is protected under Japan's publicity rights
articles.subtitle: The country's first ruling of its kind backs voice actor Kenjiro Tsuda over TikTok videos using an AI voice similar to his, though the court dismissed his demand to take them down.
articles.body:
A Tokyo court has ruled that a person's voice is protected under Japan's publicity rights, in the country's first such decision. The case was brought by the voice actor Kenjiro Tsuda, known for roles in Jujutsu Kaisen and Yu-Gi-Oh!, over TikTok videos narrated by an AI voice similar to his.

The district court dismissed Tsuda's demand for the videos to be removed because the account behind them had already been deleted. But it held that a voice can be protected when it is used specifically to exploit its commercial appeal, describing a voice as being as "symbolic of one's personality as portraits are".

The account published 188 videos between July 2024 and September 2025 and earned between ¥500,000 and ¥750,000 a month, according to the ruling. TikTok argued the narration used a "standard male voice", while the person who posted it said the AI had been trained on a friend's voice.

Japan's justice and industry ministries have published guidelines suggesting that voices may fall under publicity rights, but until now no court had recognised such a claim.
